chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
title: How the Machito band came to open the Palladium
summary: The Alma Dance Studios turned Palladium were failing; Machito, asking if the owner was prejudiced, proposed mixing audiences in a segregated era.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Okay, at that time in '49, the Palladium seemed to be going strong. I have overlooked the foundation of the Palladium, when it started in '47. How did that come about? I know the Machito orchestra was the first one to open up the Palladium. For historic reasons, I'd like you to give us that story now.
Well, let me tell you. That particular place had the same operation of Roseland ballroom and the Arcadia.
It was called Alma Dance Studios at the time.

Right, so we was so popular in the nightclub scene that - and then we was at the Concord Hotel, was one of the all year around summer resorts, still the best, the biggest in the whole world, forty-five or fifty thousand people; so considering those people live in New York State, during the summer they go to the mount. From there they come back to New York City. In those days, Long Island was as spread out as it is today, so the people were living in New York so they considered that if they hired Machito or whoever was popular in that particular time, would draw people to that particular ballroom that never had the power the Arcadia had because they was places well-built, with good bands, good behavior. They had control, everything high-class.

Roseland is still the finest ballroom in the whole world, so they was considered what Machito could be a good thing all year because we are going to enrich our clientele with all the type of people. So when we started at Palladium, naturally, the people that was there they don't know us because that was a ballroom dances; so really I was disgusted because I was success(ful) practically in every part that we appear and you get used to see a lot of people when you work, so that we were kind of, you know, gee. I feel like get out of the place. So one day I went to get paid and the owner, the one to - was the administrator says: "Machito, gee, we are in trouble. We are not doing business like we are supposed to do and we paying you a good money", whatever, and I

said the guy: yes, yes, certainly, and then I didn't think twice to what I am going to say, I was younger, and I said: Are you prejudiced? He said: "No, Machito, how could I be prejudiced when your band is all black people and Spanish people. How could I be prejudiced? If I was prejudiced, you won't be here". I say: Okay, I had an idea, why we don't change the policy of mixing up. It wasn't yet the late Kennedy and Martin Luther King, there was nothing.
Yeah, there was no integration yet.

No was integration yet, so it was, you know, something taboo; and I said; don't worry, the people that we going to bring here behave like human beings, like anybody else. So I went to 110th and 5th Ave. and found Federico Pagani - they used to run dances with us and he was the owner or the director, before, of the Happy Boys, it was a very popular band before me - so he wasn't doing anything.
